newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-PRIDE AT THE STAKE IN MADRID'S LEAGUE SHOWDOWN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PRIDE AT THE STAKE IN MADRID'S LEAGUE SHOWDOWN.

text.p: Real Madrid need just a point from Saturday's home game with Atletico to clinch their 27th Spanish league title.
Atletico's last league victory over their Madrid neighbours was in 1992, and they have nothing left to play for this season.
But calling Real's task straightforward would be to underestimate both the strength of the Atletico line-up and the passions generated by the match.
"We aren't playing for anything, just the possibility to finish fourth and above all pride," said Atletico midfielder Jose Luis Caminero, who began his career at Real.
"I hope to give them back the 4-1 that they put past us in the earlier fixture," Caminero said.
Atletico grabbed a first-half lead, and looked set to take the points after Real striker Predrag Mijatovic was sent off.
But Real teenager Raul Gonzalez played the match of his life and capped an extraordinary performance with a memorable individual goal.
For Atletico fans the defeat was a particularly bitter blow, as Raul had belonged to the club before the junior sides were scrapped as a cost-cutting measure.
Saturday could be another black day for the Atletico clan.

Real supporters are already preparing a 4 km (2.5 miles) triumphal march from the mighty Bernabeu stadium down Madrid's central avenue to the Cibeles fountain, a traditional focus of victory celebrations.
But some fans are painfully aware that overconfidence cost their side successive titles in last-match slipups at Tenerife.
The defeats handed the championship to arch-rivals Barcelona, the only side with a chance if Real stumble.
Barcelona would then have to beat Betis on Sunday, win again at Rayo Vallecano the following weekend, and see Real lose at Celta Vigo.
It's a chain of events that might seem unlikely.
But after squandering a 10-point lead, it would be a real test of nerves for the Real players to go into the last game of the season still needing a result.
If it goes that far, Celta are unlikely to need any extra motivation as they are currently fighting relegation.
But the potential lack of motivation felt by the eight first division teams left with nothing to play for has resurrected an old controversy in Spain over bonus payments to third parties.
Such payments are prohibited by the Spanish Football Federation, but nobody denies that the practice is widespread.
After the 2-1 defeat at Hercules two weeks ago, many Barcelona fans felt their opponents had fought with unusual determination for a side already condemned to relegation.

The Spanish press has repeatedly claimed that Atletico players will share 250 million pesetas ($1.72 million) if they beat Real, and that a similar amount will be offered to the Celta squad if the league is still up for grabs next weekend.
Caminero has said publicly that he wouldn't mind receiving bonuses, while Joan Gaspart said he would happily pay them once he leaves his post as Barcelona vice-president.
